options.text: BSBI appends doc_ids directly to hash-map postings lists, causing memory fragmentation

questions.explanationMd: BSBI depends on a global term-to-termID mapping, whereas SPIMI can build term dictionaries directly within blocks and avoid this global dictionary requirement.

questions.questionMd: Using a permuterm index, how is the wildcard query `*tion` translated before performing a dictionary lookup?

options.label: A
options.text: It is decomposed into k-grams and an intersection query is run against the k-gram index

options.label: B
options.text: It is reversed to `noit*` and a suffix scan is performed on the dictionary

options.label: C
options.text: It is rotated to `tion$*` and then a prefix lookup is performed on `tion$`

options.label: D
options.text: It is padded to `$*tion$` and an exact match is performed in the permuterm dictionary

questions.explanationMd: In a permuterm index, the term is imagined with `$`; moving the wildcard to the end turns `*tion` into a prefix search for `tion$`.

questions.questionMd: A student runs a Porter stemmer and observes that both `"universe"` and `"university"` produce the stem `"univers"`. This is an example of which failure mode?

options.label: A
options.text: Under-stemming, which reduces retrieval recall

options.label: B
options.text: Accent folding, which merges morphologically unrelated forms

options.label: C
options.text: Incorrect case folding applied before stemming

options.label: D
options.text: Over-stemming, which reduces retrieval precision

questions.explanationMd: Over-stemming incorrectly merges distinct terms, which can retrieve irrelevant documents and reduce precision.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, the NLTK WordNetLemmatizer called on the word `"ran"` without providing a POS tag will produce which incorrect output?

options.label: A
options.text: `"go"`, because it links irregular verb forms through WordNet

options.label: B
options.text: `"runn"`, because it applies a heuristic suffix-stripping rule

options.label: C
options.text: `"run"`, because it correctly identifies the past tense

options.label: D
options.text: `"ran"` unchanged, because it defaults to treating the word as a noun

questions.explanationMd: Without a POS tag, WordNetLemmatizer defaults to noun behavior, so it does not convert the past-tense verb `ran` to `run`.

questions.questionMd: Document A has 1000 tokens and mentions `"space"` 10 times. Document B has 100 tokens and mentions `"space"` 5 times. Which claim about TF-IDF scoring is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Both documents receive identical TF-IDF scores because IDF is the same for both

options.label: B
options.text: Document A scores higher because raw term count always dominates TF-IDF computation

options.label: C
options.text: Document B scores higher because its relative term frequency (5%) exceeds Document A's (1%)

options.label: D
options.text: Document A scores higher because a larger document contains more contextual evidence

questions.explanationMd: When term frequency is considered relative to document length or normalized, 5 occurrences in 100 tokens is stronger evidence than 10 occurrences in 1000 tokens.

questions.questionMd: After applying the full preprocessing pipeline (tokenize → lowercase → stopword removal → Porter stemming) to the input `"The astronauts ORBITING the International Space Station"`, which term in the output best illustrates a known over-stemming problem?

options.label: A
options.text: `"intern"` produced from `"International"`

options.label: B
options.text: `"astronaut"` produced from `"astronauts"`

options.label: C
options.text: `"space"` produced from `"Space"`

options.label: D
options.text: `"station"` produced from `"Station"`

questions.explanationMd: Porter stemming can reduce `international` to `intern`, which is a misleading merge with the word `intern` and is an over-stemming example.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, where do the document frequency (`df`) values required for both TF-IDF and BM25 computation come from at retrieval time?

options.label: A
options.text: From the inverted index constructed during indexing, specifically from the length of each term's postings list

options.label: B
options.text: From a separate per-document frequency table computed fresh at query time by scanning the corpus

options.label: C
options.text: From the average document length statistic `avgdl` stored alongside the inverted index

options.label: D
options.text: From the query itself, by counting how many query terms appear in a predefined stopword list

questions.explanationMd: The inverted index stores a postings list for each term; the number of documents in that list gives the document frequency.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between a token, a type, and a term?

options.label: A
options.text: A token is one occurrence in text; a type is a unique word form; a term is a normalized type entering the index

options.label: B
options.text: A token and a type are interchangeable; a term is produced only after stopword removal

options.label: C
options.text: A term is one occurrence in text; a token is a unique normalized form; a type is what enters the index

options.label: D
options.text: A type is one occurrence in text; a token is a unique word form; a term is produced by tokenization

questions.explanationMd: Tokens are individual occurrences, types are distinct surface forms, and terms are normalized forms used in the index.

questions.questionMd: In SMART notation, the scheme `lnc.ltc` specifies which combination of weighting choices for documents and queries respectively?

options.label: A
options.text: Documents use natural TF, cosine normalization, no IDF; queries use log-TF, IDF, cosine normalization

options.label: B
options.text: Documents use log-TF, natural IDF, cosine normalization; queries use log-TF, no IDF, cosine normalization

options.label: C
options.text: Documents use log-TF, no IDF, no normalization; queries use log-TF, standard IDF, cosine normalization

options.label: D
options.text: Documents use log-TF, no IDF, cosine normalization; queries use log-TF, standard IDF, cosine normalization

questions.explanationMd: In `lnc.ltc`, documents use logarithmic TF, no IDF, and cosine normalization; queries use logarithmic TF, IDF, and cosine normalization.

questions.questionMd: Why is Normalized DCG (NDCG) preferred over raw DCG when comparing results across multiple queries?

options.label: A
options.text: NDCG normalizes by the ideal DCG so all queries map to `[0,1]`

options.label: B
options.text: NDCG uses binary relevance labels, which are easier to collect than the graded labels required by raw DCG

options.label: C
options.text: Raw DCG rewards retrieving more documents, while NDCG penalizes systems that return more than `k` results

options.label: D
options.text: NDCG applies a stricter position discount than DCG, making it more sensitive to early retrieval errors

questions.explanationMd: NDCG divides DCG by the ideal DCG for that query, making scores comparable across queries with different relevance distributions.

questions.questionMd: As the raw term frequency `tf` in a document increases toward infinity, what value does the BM25 TF saturation function `tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1)` approach?

options.label: A
options.text: The value `k1 + 1`, which is the asymptotic maximum that the saturation function never exceeds

options.label: B
options.text: The value `k1`, which acts as a hard ceiling on TF contributions

options.label: C
options.text: The value `tf`, meaning the saturation function converges back to raw TF at very high counts

options.label: D
options.text: The value `1`, because the saturation function is normalized to the range `[0, 1]`

questions.explanationMd: As `tf` becomes very large, the leading `tf` terms dominate the numerator and denominator, so the expression approaches `k1 + 1`.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, in which of the following situations does the Bag-of-Words assumption most clearly lead to incorrect retrieval behavior?

options.label: A
options.text: When two documents have the same vocabulary size, because BoW cannot differentiate their vectors

options.label: B
options.text: When query terms appear frequently in the same document, because BoW over-weights high-frequency terms

options.label: C
options.text: When a query contains negation such as `"not relevant"`

options.label: D
options.text: When query terms are stopwords, because BoW assigns them the same weight as content terms

questions.explanationMd: Bag-of-Words ignores word order and syntax, so it can mishandle negation; `not relevant` may be treated similarly to `relevant`.

questions.questionMd: Which sequence correctly describes the three-stage spelling correction pipeline?

options.label: A
options.text: Jaccard similarity filtering → k-gram candidate retrieval → edit distance ranking.

options.label: B
options.text: K-gram candidate retrieval → edit distance ranking → Jaccard similarity filtering.

options.label: C
options.text: K-gram candidate retrieval → Jaccard similarity filtering → edit distance ranking.

options.label: D
options.text: Edit distance ranking → Jaccard similarity filtering → k-gram candidate retrieval.

questions.explanationMd: The usual pipeline first retrieves candidates using k-grams, filters cheaply with Jaccard similarity, then ranks the remaining candidates by edit distance.

questions.questionMd: Heap's Law describes how vocabulary size `V` grows with the total number of tokens `N` in a corpus. Which statement correctly characterizes this growth?

options.label: A
options.text: Vocabulary grows sub-linearly and never fully stops growing

options.label: B
options.text: Vocabulary grows linearly, adding a fixed number of new terms per document

options.label: C
options.text: Vocabulary grows exponentially in proportion to the square of `N`

options.label: D
options.text: Vocabulary growth stops once the corpus exceeds a threshold size

questions.explanationMd: Heap's Law states `V = kN^β` with `0 < β < 1`, so vocabulary growth is sub-linear but continues as the corpus grows.

questions.questionMd: In Apache Lucene's segment-based architecture, what happens when a document is updated?

options.label: A
options.text: The document is moved to a special update buffer that replaces the original segment during the next merge.

options.label: B
options.text: All segments containing that document are merged immediately to apply the update atomically.

options.label: C
options.text: The existing segment is opened and the document's fields are overwritten in place.

options.label: D
options.text: The old document is marked as deleted and the updated version is written as a new entry.

questions.explanationMd: Lucene segments are immutable. An update is handled as a delete of the old document plus adding the new version in a new segment entry.

questions.questionMd: Which expression correctly gives the cosine similarity between document vector `d` and query vector `q`?
questions.explanationMd: Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the vector norms.

questions.questionMd: Three queries yield Average Precision scores of 0.72, 0.45, and 0.38 for a system. What is the MAP?

options.label: B
options.text: 1.550, because MAP sums the AP values without dividing by the number of queries.

options.label: C
options.text: 0.720, because MAP reports the highest AP score across all queries.

options.label: D
options.text: 0.550, computed as the median of the three AP values.

questions.explanationMd: MAP is the arithmetic mean of Average Precision values across queries: `(0.72 + 0.45 + 0.38) / 3 = 0.517`.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following inputs causes whitespace tokenization to produce an incorrect or problematic result?

options.label: A
options.text: "search" treated as a single token

options.label: B
options.text: "nlp.stanford.edu" treated as a single token

options.label: C
options.text: "running" treated as a single token

options.label: D
options.text: "cat" treated as a single token

questions.explanationMd: Whitespace tokenization splits only on spaces, so a URL-like string such as `nlp.stanford.edu` remains one token even though punctuation may need special handling.

questions.questionMd: After intersecting k-gram postings to resolve a wildcard query, why is a mandatory post-filtering step required?

options.label: A
options.text: K-gram postings lists are unsorted, so the intersection result contains duplicate terms.

options.label: B
options.text: Post-filtering converts k-gram integer IDs back into human-readable vocabulary terms.

options.label: C
options.text: The k-gram intersection can only retrieve terms from a single partition of the vocabulary at a time.

options.label: D
options.text: K-gram matching is a necessary but not sufficient condition.

questions.explanationMd: A term may contain all required k-grams but still fail the wildcard pattern, so candidates must be checked against the original wildcard expression.

questions.questionMd: A document contains 200 tokens, and the term `orbit` appears 4 times. What is the Term Frequency (TF) of `orbit` in this document?
questions.explanationMd: Using normalized term frequency, `TF = 4 / 200 = 0.02`.

questions.questionMd: Lucene uses a Finite State Transducer (FST) as its term dictionary structure. What property makes the FST particularly well-suited for this role?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a hash map that maps each term to its document frequency, enabling O(1) IDF lookups during scoring.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a compact, memory-efficient graph that supports `O(len)` prefix and suffix lookups on the sorted term list.

options.label: C
options.text: It stores postings lists in columnar format so that aggregations can be computed without loading all term data into RAM.

options.label: D
options.text: It uses a B-tree structure to guarantee `O(log n)` insertion time when new terms are added to a mutable segment.

questions.explanationMd: FSTs compactly represent sorted terms and support efficient prefix-style traversal, making them suitable for term dictionaries.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a known limitation of the probabilistic IDF formula `log((N - df) / df)` as noted in the lecture?

options.label: A
options.text: The formula can produce negative values, requiring careful handling in implementations.

options.label: B
options.text: The formula cannot be computed when the document frequency is greater than 1.

options.label: C
options.text: The formula always returns the same value regardless of the collection size `N`.

options.label: D
options.text: The formula doubles the IDF value of any term whose document frequency exceeds `N/2`.

questions.explanationMd: When `df > N/2`, `(N - df) / df` is less than 1, so its logarithm is negative.

questions.questionMd: What is the effect of setting the BM25 parameter `k1` to a very large value, approaching infinity?

options.label: A
options.text: TF saturation disappears and the scoring approaches raw TF with no diminishing returns.

options.label: B
options.text: The BM25 score becomes equivalent to a binary Boolean match signal.

options.label: C
options.text: The IDF component is scaled down and rare terms receive lower weights.

options.label: D
options.text: Length normalization is disabled and all documents are treated as having equal length.

questions.explanationMd: As `k1` grows very large, the BM25 TF component saturates less and behaves more like raw term frequency.

questions.questionMd: When two sorted postings lists are merged with OR and both pointers point to the same document ID, what is the correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: Emit the document ID once and advance both pointers.

options.label: B
options.text: Emit the document ID twice to reflect it appears in both lists and advance both pointers.

options.label: C
options.text: Skip the document ID entirely because it indicates an AND match, not an OR match.

options.label: D
options.text: Emit the document ID once and advance only the pointer into the shorter list.

questions.explanationMd: For OR, a document appearing in both lists is still output once; advancing both pointers avoids duplicates.

questions.questionMd: A user searches `automobile fuel efficiency`, but the most relevant document uses only the phrases `car gas mileage` and `vehicle consumption`. What problem does this scenario illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: The precision-recall tradeoff: retrieving more documents lowers average result quality.

options.label: B
options.text: The vocabulary mismatch problem: lexical overlap is zero despite near-identical meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: The stopword problem: common function words are masking the discriminating content terms.

options.label: D
options.text: The corpus freshness problem: the index has not been updated to include recent terminology.

questions.explanationMd: The query and relevant document use different words for the same concepts, so lexical matching fails despite semantic similarity.

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch query uses `fields`: [`title^3`, `body^1`] inside a `multi_match` clause. What does the `^3` notation mean for the `title` field?

options.label: A
options.text: A match in the title field contributes three times more to the relevance score than an equivalent match in the body field.

options.label: B
options.text: OpenSearch searches the title field three times before falling back to the body field.

options.label: C
options.text: The title field is indexed three times to increase recall for title matches.

options.label: D
options.text: The query requires at least three matching terms in the title field before the document is considered a candidate.

questions.explanationMd: The caret notation applies a boost; `title^3` weights title matches three times more than the unboosted field.

questions.questionMd: According to SMART notation, which formula defines the logarithmic TF variant, symbol `l`, for a term with a non-zero count?

options.label: B
options.text: `1 + log(tf)`

options.label: C
options.text: `tf / (1 + log(tf))`

options.label: D
options.text: `log(tf) - 1`

questions.explanationMd: In SMART notation, the logarithmic TF weighting uses `1 + log(tf)` for non-zero term frequency.

questions.questionMd: A term is best defined as which of the following in the context of information retrieval indexing?

options.label: A
options.text: Any single occurrence of a word anywhere in a document collection

options.label: B
options.text: A normalized type that survives all preprocessing steps and enters the inverted index

options.label: C
options.text: A unique word form in the vocabulary before any normalization is applied

options.label: D
options.text: A token produced by splitting raw text on whitespace boundaries

questions.explanationMd: A term is the normalized representation that is actually indexed after tokenization and preprocessing such as lowercasing, stopword removal, or stemming.

questions.questionMd: Under which condition do skip pointers provide the greatest reduction in comparisons during an AND merge?

options.label: A
options.text: When both postings lists have identical length.

options.label: B
options.text: When both postings lists contain more than 10,000 entries.

options.label: C
options.text: When the two postings lists are very unequal in length.

options.label: D
options.text: When the query contains three or more AND operands.

questions.explanationMd: Skip pointers are most useful when one list can jump over many entries while trying to catch up to the other list.

questions.questionMd: Using the standard IDF formula taught in lecture, how is `IDF(t)` computed for a term `t` given a collection of `N` documents where `t` appears in `df(t)` of them?

options.label: A
options.text: `log(N / df(t))`

options.label: B
options.text: `log(df(t) / N)`

options.label: C
options.text: `N / df(t)`

options.label: D
options.text: `log(N * df(t))`

questions.explanationMd: Standard IDF increases for rare terms and is commonly computed as `log(N / df(t))`.

questions.questionMd: In the Vector Space Model, why are document vectors described as sparse?

options.label: A
options.text: Vectors are sparse because cosine normalization sets most small weights to zero during L2 normalization.

options.label: B
options.text: Sparsity arises because IDF values are rounded to zero for any term with document frequency above a threshold.

options.label: C
options.text: Document vectors are sparse because only the top-k highest-weighted terms are stored to save memory.

options.label: D
options.text: Most vocabulary terms do not appear in any given document.

questions.explanationMd: A document contains only a small subset of the full vocabulary, so most vector dimensions are zero.

questions.questionMd: Which formula correctly defines Precision in an information retrieval evaluation context?

options.label: A
options.text: `|Relevant ∩ Retrieved| / |Relevant|`

options.label: B
options.text: `|Relevant| / (|Relevant| + |Retrieved|)`

options.label: C
options.text: `|Retrieved| / |Relevant|`

options.label: D
options.text: `|Relevant ∩ Retrieved| / |Retrieved|`

questions.explanationMd: Precision is the fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant.

questions.questionMd: How does lemmatization handle the word `better` when supplied with the correct POS tag indicating it is an adjective?

options.label: A
options.text: It maps `better` to `bett` by stripping the comparative suffix.

options.label: B
options.text: It returns `better` unchanged because it is already a base-form adjective.

options.label: C
options.text: It maps `better` to `best` as the superlative base form.

options.label: D
options.text: It maps `better` to `good`.

questions.explanationMd: With adjective POS information, lemmatization can map the comparative form `better` to the lemma `good`.

questions.questionMd: Why does OpenSearch periodically merge smaller Lucene segments into larger ones in the background?

options.label: A
options.text: Merging segments compresses stored document content, reducing disk storage requirements significantly.

options.label: B
options.text: Fewer, larger segments reduce the number of files that must be opened and scanned during a query.

options.label: C
options.text: The merge process recalculates BM25 scores globally, correcting the IDF discrepancy across shards.

options.label: D
options.text: Merging allows the primary shard count to grow dynamically without requiring a full reindex.

questions.explanationMd: Segment merging reduces the number of small segments searched, improving query efficiency and housekeeping.

questions.questionMd: When the two postings lists being merged with skip pointers have approximately equal lengths, what effect do skip pointers have on performance?

options.label: A
options.text: The overhead of checking skip conditions at each step can make performance marginally worse than the naive merge.

options.label: B
options.text: Skip pointers have no effect at all because they are only stored for lists longer than 10,000 entries.

options.label: C
options.text: Skip pointers provide the largest speedup because both lists benefit equally from jumping ahead.

options.label: D
options.text: The merge terminates earlier than the naive case because both lists can skip simultaneously.

questions.explanationMd: When lists are similar in length, there may be fewer useful jumps, so checking skip conditions can add slight overhead.

questions.questionMd: Mean Average Precision (MAP) penalizes a system that fails to retrieve some relevant documents. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: Unretrieved documents are assigned the lowest possible rank, which increases the denominator of the AP formula.

options.label: B
options.text: Relevant documents that are never retrieved contribute a precision of 0 to the AP calculation.

options.label: C
options.text: MAP is computed only over queries where the system retrieved at least one relevant document, excluding all others.

options.label: D
options.text: MAP applies a log-discount to later ranks, making missing documents proportionally more costly.

questions.explanationMd: Average Precision averages precision contributions over all relevant documents; unretrieved relevant documents contribute zero.

questions.questionMd: In the three-stage spelling correction pipeline, what is the primary purpose of the Jaccard similarity filtering stage?

options.label: A
options.text: To apply context-sensitive correction by comparing candidates against a bigram language model

options.label: B
options.text: To eliminate most implausible candidates cheaply before the expensive edit distance computation

options.label: C
options.text: To rank the final correction suggestions by their phonetic similarity to the misspelled word

options.label: D
options.text: To build the initial candidate set by finding all vocabulary terms sharing at least one k-gram

questions.explanationMd: Jaccard filtering is a cheap candidate-pruning step. It reduces the number of terms that must be passed to the more expensive edit-distance calculation.

questions.questionMd: Why does the Vector Space Model use cosine similarity rather than Euclidean distance to compare document and query vectors?

options.label: A
options.text: Euclidean distance produces values outside the range [0, 1], making it impossible to rank documents consistently

options.label: B
options.text: Euclidean distance would make a long document seem very different from a short one covering the same topics

options.label: C
options.text: Euclidean distance cannot be computed for high-dimensional vectors, whereas cosine similarity is defined for any number of dimensions

options.label: D
options.text: Cosine similarity is always faster to compute than Euclidean distance for sparse TF-IDF vectors

questions.explanationMd: Euclidean distance is sensitive to vector magnitude. A long and a short document about the same topic may be far apart by distance even if their term distributions are similar.

questions.questionMd: In the positional index approach to phrase queries, what is the role of the first phase?

options.label: A
options.text: It uses an AND merge.

options.label: B
options.text: It verifies that query terms appear at consecutive positions in each document.

options.label: C
options.text: It resolves wildcard patterns into concrete vocabulary terms using the k-gram index.

options.label: D
options.text: It applies Jaccard similarity to rank candidate documents by term overlap.

questions.explanationMd: The first phase uses an AND merge to find documents that contain all phrase terms; a later positional check verifies whether the terms occur consecutively and in order.

questions.questionMd: A developer indexes documents using the `english` analyzer, which applies Porter stemming, but accidentally uses the `standard` analyzer, no stemming, at query time. What problem will this cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The query term will not match the stemmed index tokens; for example, `shuttle` will fail to match the stored token `shuttl`.

options.label: B
options.text: OpenSearch automatically detects the mismatch and applies the index-time analyzer to query terms before searching.

options.label: C
options.text: Queries will return too many results because the standard analyzer is less selective than the English analyzer.

options.label: D
options.text: BM25 scores will be slightly lower, but all relevant documents will still be retrieved correctly.

questions.explanationMd: Index-time and query-time analysis must be compatible; otherwise query tokens may not match the normalized tokens stored in the index.

questions.questionMd: A system retrieves 5 documents for a query that has 10 relevant documents, and all 5 retrieved documents are relevant and ranked perfectly. What is the maximum possible AP for this query?

options.label: A
options.text: 0.5, because the 5 unretrieved relevant documents each contribute 0 to the AP sum.

options.label: B
options.text: 0.0, because MAP requires all relevant documents to be retrieved before assigning any credit.

options.label: C
options.text: 1.0, because every retrieved document is relevant and ranked in perfect order.

options.label: D
options.text: 0.75, because partial retrieval is penalised by a fixed 25% reduction in AP.

questions.explanationMd: AP divides by the total number of relevant documents. Five perfect retrieved relevant documents contribute 5, but the five missing relevant documents contribute 0, so AP is `5/10 = 0.5`.

questions.questionMd: After applying the full preprocessing pipeline, tokenize → lowercase → stopword removal → Porter stemming, to the input `The astronauts ORBITING the International Space Station`, which term in the output best illustrates a known over-stemming problem?

options.label: A
options.text: `station` produced from `Station`.

options.label: B
options.text: `astronaut` produced from `astronauts`.

options.label: C
options.text: `intern` produced from `International`.

options.label: D
options.text: `space` produced from `Space`.

questions.explanationMd: Porter stemming may reduce `international` to `intern`, which can conflate terms too aggressively and cause over-stemming.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following operations in OpenSearch relies on DocValues rather than the inverted index?

options.label: A
options.text: Storing the original human-readable content of a document so it can be displayed in search results.

options.label: B
options.text: Finding all documents that contain the term `laptop` in a full-text search query.

options.label: C
options.text: Sorting results by a numeric price field and computing aggregation buckets for faceted navigation.

options.label: D
options.text: Applying a Porter stemmer to tokenize and normalize query terms at search time.

questions.explanationMd: DocValues are column-oriented structures used for sorting, aggregations, and faceting on field values.

questions.questionMd: Which decade saw the introduction of the Cranfield experiments, the first systematic methodology for evaluating information retrieval systems?

options.label: A
options.text: The 1960s.

options.label: B
options.text: The 1940s.

options.label: C
options.text: The 1980s.

options.label: D
options.text: The 1970s.

questions.explanationMd: The Cranfield experiments are associated with the 1960s and helped establish systematic IR evaluation methodology.

questions.questionMd: A system achieves `NDCG@k = 1.0` for a given query. What must be true?

options.label: A
options.text: The system's ranking is identical to the ideal ranking.

options.label: B
options.text: The system's `DCG@k` equals zero, meaning no relevant documents were returned.

options.label: C
options.text: `NDCG@k = 1.0` is impossible; values are strictly bounded below 1.0 in practice.

options.label: D
options.text: The system retrieved exactly `k` documents, all of which are relevant.

questions.explanationMd: NDCG equals 1 when the ranking up to `k` achieves the ideal possible DCG for that query.

questions.questionMd: A student runs a Porter stemmer and observes that both **universe** and **university** produce the stem **univers**. This is an example of which failure mode?

options.label: A
options.text: Incorrect case folding applied before stemming

options.label: B
options.text: Over-stemming, which reduces retrieval precision

options.label: C
options.text: Under-stemming, which reduces retrieval recall

options.label: D
options.text: Accent folding, which merges morphologically unrelated forms

questions.explanationMd: Porter stemming has merged two semantically different words into the same stem. This is over-stemming and it can reduce precision by matching unrelated documents.

questions.questionMd: A developer uses `SELECT * FROM papers WHERE abstract LIKE '%heart attack%'` to find cardiology research. What is the most significant limitation of this approach compared to an IR system?

options.label: A
options.text: It returns no results for documents using the synonym "myocardial infarction".

options.label: B
options.text: It cannot filter results by publication date or author name

options.label: C
options.text: It is slower than an inverted index for corpora with fewer than one million rows

options.label: D
options.text: It requires a separate full-text parser before the SQL engine can execute

questions.explanationMd: A simple SQL `LIKE` query performs literal pattern matching and does not understand synonyms. An IR system can use analysis, expansion, or ranking to better handle vocabulary mismatch.

questions.questionMd: Which statement best captures the concept of TF saturation as modelled by BM25 and log-TF?

options.label: A
options.text: TF saturation means that once a term appears more than k1 times, it is completely ignored in scoring

options.label: B
options.text: Each additional occurrence of a term contributes progressively less to the relevance score

options.label: C
options.text: Each additional occurrence of a term contributes equally to the relevance score regardless of how many times it has already appeared

options.label: D
options.text: TF saturation increases the weight of the first occurrence of a term and sets all subsequent occurrences to zero

questions.explanationMd: TF saturation means term-frequency gains have diminishing returns. BM25 and log-TF avoid letting repeated occurrences increase the score linearly forever.

questions.questionMd: Why can a leading wildcard query such as `*tion` not be resolved efficiently using only the standard forward-sorted dictionary?

options.label: A
options.text: A forward-sorted dictionary is compressed and cannot support random access required for suffix lookups

options.label: B
options.text: A forward-sorted dictionary provides no entry point for suffix patterns

options.label: C
options.text: The forward dictionary only indexes terms of more than three characters, excluding short suffix patterns

options.label: D
options.text: Leading wildcards require positional index data that is not stored in the dictionary layer

questions.explanationMd: A forward-sorted dictionary is efficient for prefixes, not suffixes. With a leading wildcard, the known characters are at the end, so there is no direct starting point for lookup.

questions.questionMd: In the Vector Space Model (VSM), what determines the number of dimensions in a document vector?

options.label: A
options.text: The size of the vocabulary |V| of the entire collection

options.label: B
options.text: The number of documents in the collection

options.label: C
options.text: The number of tokens in the document being represented

options.label: D
options.text: The number of unique terms in the query

questions.explanationMd: In VSM, each vocabulary term corresponds to one dimension. Therefore the vector dimensionality is the collection vocabulary size `|V|`.

questions.questionMd: What is the recommended skip pointer interval for a postings list of length 400?
questions.explanationMd: A common heuristic is to place about `sqrt(P)` skip pointers for a postings list of length `P`. Since `sqrt(400)=20`, the recommended interval is 20.

questions.questionMd: A spelling corrector using a Jaccard threshold of 0.2 consistently returns no candidates for misspelled words of four characters or fewer. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: A
options.text: The k-gram index only indexes vocabulary terms of five characters or more by default

options.label: B
options.text: Edit distance computation fails on short strings because the dynamic programming table is too small

options.label: C
options.text: Short words produce very few k-grams, so Jaccard scores are inherently lower

options.label: D
options.text: Short words are automatically classified as stop words and excluded from the k-gram index

questions.explanationMd: Short strings produce very few k-grams. A small difference can therefore reduce the Jaccard score sharply, causing candidates to fall below the threshold.

questions.questionMd: Why is leading a query with a NOT operation alone considered poor practice?

options.label: A
options.text: It produces the same result as an AND query but takes longer to parse

options.label: B
options.text: It requires building a secondary inverted index from scratch at query time

options.label: C
options.text: It can only be applied after an OR merge has been completed

options.label: D
options.text: It requires scanning the entire corpus to find all document IDs not in the negated list

questions.explanationMd: A leading `NOT` defines the complement of a postings list. To compute it, the system may need to consider the full universe of document IDs.

questions.questionMd: Which organisation established TREC (Text REtrieval Conference) in 1992 to provide shared benchmarks for IR evaluation?

options.label: A
options.text: IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers)

options.label: B
options.text: ACM (Association for Computing Machinery)

options.label: C
options.text: DARPA (Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency)

options.label: D
options.text: NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)

questions.explanationMd: TREC was established by NIST to support shared evaluation tasks, test collections, and relevance judgments for information retrieval research.

questions.questionMd: Which specific problem motivated the development of the BM25F variant?

options.label: A
options.text: Standard BM25 cannot handle multi-word queries because it sums scores term by term, a limitation BM25F overcomes

options.label: B
options.text: Standard BM25 produces negative IDF values for terms with very high document frequency, which BM25F corrects

options.label: C
options.text: Standard BM25 treats a document as a single flat text field

options.label: D
options.text: Standard BM25 requires all documents in the collection to have the same length, which BM25F relaxes with per-document normalization

questions.explanationMd: BM25F extends BM25 to handle structured documents with multiple fields, such as title, body, and anchor text, instead of treating everything as one flat field.

questions.questionMd: Given the ranked list **R, I, I, R, R** (`R = relevant`, `I = irrelevant`), what is the Average Precision (AP)?
questions.explanationMd: Relevant documents occur at ranks 1, 4, and 5. AP is `(P@1 + P@4 + P@5)/3 = (1 + 0.5 + 0.6)/3 = 0.700`.

questions.questionMd: The Probability Ranking Principle (PRP), which motivates BM25, states that documents should be ranked according to which criterion?

options.label: A
options.text: Decreasing probability of relevance given the document and query

options.label: B
options.text: Decreasing term frequency summed across all query terms

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing document frequency of the query terms in the collection

options.label: D
options.text: Decreasing document length relative to the collection average

questions.explanationMd: PRP says documents should be ordered by decreasing probability of relevance for the given query. BM25 is motivated by this probabilistic ranking view.

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch query uses `{ "fuzzy": { "title": { "value": "shudtle", "fuzziness": "AUTO" } } }`. Which concept from earlier in the course does this query clause directly implement at the search engine level?

options.label: A
options.text: Phonetic similarity hashing, which maps words that sound alike to the same hash bucket for retrieval.

options.label: B
options.text: Wildcard pattern expansion, which generates all terms matching a prefix or suffix pattern before scoring.

options.label: C
options.text: Edit distance (Levenshtein distance) based spelling correction.

options.label: D
options.text: Porter stemming, which normalizes inflected word forms to a common root before index lookup.

questions.explanationMd: OpenSearch fuzzy matching uses edit-distance style matching, commonly Levenshtein distance, to find terms close to the misspelled query term.

questions.questionMd: A colleague argues that MAP is always preferable to NDCG@k because MAP considers the entire ranked list rather than a cutoff. Which counter-argument best explains a key limitation of MAP?

options.label: A
options.text: MAP penalises systems that retrieve more than k documents, making deep retrieval unfair

options.label: B
options.text: MAP is only defined for navigational queries where exactly one relevant document exists

options.label: C
options.text: MAP requires a larger query set than NDCG@k to produce stable estimates

options.label: D
options.text: MAP assumes binary relevance

questions.explanationMd: MAP is based on binary relevance judgments. NDCG can naturally use graded relevance, so it can distinguish highly relevant from partially relevant documents.

questions.questionMd: Given two k-gram sets A and B, which expression correctly computes their Jaccard similarity?
questions.explanationMd: Jaccard similarity is the size of the intersection divided by the size of the union of the two sets.

questions.questionMd: In the Boolean retrieval model, which operator precedence order is correct when no parentheses are used?

options.label: A
options.text: AND is evaluated first, then NOT, then OR

options.label: B
options.text: NOT is evaluated first, then AND, then OR

options.label: C
options.text: NOT and AND share equal precedence and are evaluated before OR

options.label: D
options.text: OR is evaluated first, then AND, then NOT

questions.explanationMd: The standard precedence order is `NOT` first, then `AND`, then `OR`, unless parentheses override it.

questions.questionMd: What is the typical relationship between Precision and Recall as more documents are retrieved?

options.label: A
options.text: Precision tends to decrease as Recall increases, reflecting a fundamental tradeoff

options.label: B
options.text: Both Precision and Recall increase together as more documents are retrieved

options.label: C
options.text: Precision stays constant while Recall increases

options.label: D
options.text: Recall decreases as Precision increases, because early ranks contain the best results

questions.explanationMd: Retrieving more documents usually finds more relevant documents, increasing recall, but also adds more nonrelevant documents, which tends to lower precision.

questions.questionMd: When optimizing a multi-term AND query by sorting operands in order of ascending document frequency, what is the primary benefit?

options.label: A
options.text: The total number of postings lists loaded into memory is reduced

options.label: B
options.text: Intermediate result sets shrink fastest when processing begins with the rarest terms

options.label: C
options.text: Skip pointers become unnecessary for the remaining operations

options.label: D
options.text: The OR merge step is eliminated from the query plan

questions.explanationMd: For an AND query, starting with the rarest terms produces smaller intermediate intersections early, reducing later comparison work.

questions.questionMd: In the Average Precision formula `AP = (1/R) x Σ P@k`, what does the summation run over?

options.label: A
options.text: The top-k positions specified by the evaluation cutoff

options.label: B
options.text: All rank positions from 1 to the total number of retrieved documents

options.label: C
options.text: Only the rank positions k where the retrieved document is relevant

options.label: D
options.text: All positions where the retrieved document is irrelevant, as a penalty term

questions.explanationMd: Average Precision averages precision values only at ranks where a relevant document is retrieved.

questions.questionMd: In the IR triangle model, which concept sits at the centre connecting the query, the document, and the information need?

options.label: A
options.text: Vocabulary

options.label: B
options.text: Ranking

options.label: C
options.text: Precision

options.label: D
options.text: Relevance

questions.explanationMd: Relevance connects the user's information need, the query representation, and the documents returned by the system.

questions.questionMd: A student searches for **flight delays snow**. Their actual need is to understand why winter weather disrupts air travel. What does this example best illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: Queries and information needs are equivalent when the user is precise

options.label: B
options.text: A query is always a lossy compression of the underlying information need

options.label: C
options.text: Search engines require queries to match document text exactly

options.label: D
options.text: Information needs can be fully captured in two or three words

questions.explanationMd: A short query is only an imperfect expression of a broader information need. It often omits context, intent, and desired explanation.

questions.questionMd: A developer wants to build a faceted navigation sidebar that counts how many products belong to each category (e.g., **Electronics: 120**, **Clothing: 85**). Which field type should the category field use in the OpenSearch mapping?

options.label: A
options.text: text, because it supports full-text analysis which enables partial matching of category names.

options.label: B
options.text: keyword, because it stores exact unanalyzed values that can be used in terms aggregations.

options.label: C
options.text: integer, because aggregation requires numeric fields to produce accurate bucket counts.

options.label: D
options.text: text with the english analyzer, so that category names are stemmed before aggregation.

questions.explanationMd: A `keyword` field stores exact values and is appropriate for terms aggregations, faceting, and category counts.

questions.questionMd: Case folding converts **Apple** to **apple** during normalization. According to the lecture, which specific example demonstrates that lowercasing is NOT always a safe operation?

options.label: A
options.text: "Apple" (company name) vs. "apple" (the fruit) carry different meanings

options.label: B
options.text: "NASA" should always be lowercased to "nasa" for consistency

options.label: C
options.text: "Running" and "running" should always be treated as the same term

options.label: D
options.text: Accent folding should always be performed before case folding

questions.explanationMd: Lowercasing can remove meaningful distinctions. `Apple` as a company and `apple` as a fruit are different entities even though their lowercase forms match.

questions.questionMd: According to SMART notation, which formula defines the logarithmic TF variant (symbol `l`) for a term with a non-zero count?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.explanationMd: In SMART notation, the logarithmic TF variant `l` is defined as `1 + log(tf)` for non-zero term frequency.

questions.questionMd: R-Precision is defined as Precision computed at rank `R`, where `R` is which quantity?

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: The total number of relevant documents for that query in the collection

options.label: C
options.text: The rank of the first relevant document returned by the system

options.label: D
options.text: The ratio of retrieved documents to total collection size

questions.explanationMd: R-Precision evaluates precision at the cutoff equal to the number of relevant documents for that query.

questions.questionMd: A developer wants to build a faceted navigation sidebar that counts how many products belong to each category, such as `Electronics: 120` and `Clothing: 85`. Which field type should the category field use in the OpenSearch mapping?

questions.questionMd: Using the DCG formula `rel_i / log₂(i + 1)`, what is the position discount factor applied to a document at rank 2?

options.label: A
options.text: Exactly 1.00, because rank 2 is still in the top results and receives no discount

options.text: Exactly 0.50, because rank 2 halves the contribution relative to rank 1

questions.questionMd: In a standard TREC qrels file, each line maps a `(query_id, doc_id)` pair to a relevance label. What does a grade of 0 in a graded qrels file signify?

options.label: A

options.label: D
options.text: The document was judged by a human assessor and found to be irrelevant to the query

questions.explanationMd: A qrels grade of 0 means the document was assessed and judged non-relevant.

questions.questionMd: Expanding a search to retrieve more candidate documents generally increases recall. What is the typical effect on precision?

options.label: A
options.text: Precision tends to decrease because more irrelevant documents enter the result set

options.label: B
options.text: Precision and recall always move in the same direction under any retrieval strategy

options.label: C
options.text: Precision increases proportionally because a larger result set exposes more relevant documents

options.label: D
options.text: Precision is unaffected because it is computed over only the relevant documents retrieved

questions.explanationMd: Broadening retrieval often captures more relevant documents but also introduces more non-relevant ones, reducing precision.

questions.questionMd: A corpus contains 1000 documents, and the term `quasar` appears in exactly 50 of them. Applying the formula `IDF(t) = log(N / df(t))`, what is the IDF of `quasar`?
questions.explanationMd: `N/df = 1000/50 = 20`, so the IDF is `log(20)`, approximately 3.0 with natural log.

questions.questionMd: Given two sorted postings lists of lengths `m` and `n`, what is the time complexity of the two-pointer AND merge algorithm?

options.label: A

options.label: B

questions.explanationMd: Each pointer only moves forward through its list, so the total work is linear in the two list lengths.

questions.questionMd: In TREC-style evaluation, the pooling method is used to reduce annotation cost. What known bias does this approach introduce?

questions.explanationMd: Unjudged documents outside the pool are commonly treated as non-relevant during evaluation, which can penalize systems finding novel relevant documents.

questions.questionMd: In an OpenSearch bool query, which clause excludes matching documents from the result set without contributing to the relevance score of remaining documents?

questions.questionMd: Which statement correctly describes a known limitation of offline IR evaluation using test collections?

options.label: A

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture's compression data, combining gap encoding with VB encoding on a typical postings list achieves what overall compression factor compared to storing raw int32 doc_ids?

questions.questionMd: The log-average TF variant (symbol `L`) in SMART notation is defined as which of the following expressions?

questions.questionMd: What is the time complexity of BSBI expressed in terms of `T`, the total number of token occurrences in the corpus?

questions.questionMd: Why does a term that appears in every document in a corpus receive an IDF score of zero?

questions.questionMd: Why do high-frequency terms with large document frequency achieve better compression ratios than rare terms when gap encoding combined with VB encoding is applied?

questions.questionMd: What practical implication does Zipf's Law have for the design of a stopword list?

questions.questionMd: OpenSearch uses the formula `shard_id = hash(document_id) mod num_primary_shards` to decide where to store a document. What is the primary consequence of this routing mechanism?

questions.questionMd: Embedding skip pointers into a postings list at index build time introduces which tradeoff?

options.text: The index occupies more storage space in exchange for faster AND merge performance

questions.explanationMd: Skip pointers add extra data to the index but can speed up postings intersections.

questions.questionMd: When performing an OR merge on two sorted postings lists of lengths `m` and `n`, which statement correctly describes the size of the result?

options.label: A
options.text: The result is always at least as large as the longer of the two input lists

options.label: B
options.text: The result is always exactly `m + n`

options.label: C
options.text: The result is always equal to the shorter list's length

options.label: D
options.text: The result is always smaller than both input lists

questions.explanationMd: A union must contain all documents from the larger list, plus any additional unique documents from the other list.

questions.questionMd: A retrieval system returns 10 documents in response to a query. Seven of them are relevant. The corpus contains 20 relevant documents in total. What are the precision and recall values?

options.label: A
options.text: Precision = 0.35, Recall = 0.35

options.label: B
options.text: Precision = 0.35, Recall = 0.7

options.label: C
options.text: Precision = 0.7, Recall = 0.7

options.label: D
options.text: Precision = 0.7, Recall = 0.35

questions.explanationMd: Precision is `7/10 = 0.7`; recall is `7/20 = 0.35`.

questions.questionMd: Zipf's Law states that the frequency of the `r`-th most common word is proportional to `1/r`. If the most frequent term in a corpus appears 10,000 times, approximately how often does the 100th most frequent term appear?

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately 1,000 times

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 10 times

options.label: C
options.text: Approximately 100 times

options.label: D
options.text: Approximately 5,000 times

questions.explanationMd: Zipf's Law gives `10000 / 100 = 100`.

questions.questionMd: Why is raw term frequency (TF) considered a biased signal when comparing documents of different lengths?

options.label: A
options.text: Longer documents tend to accumulate higher raw TF values

options.label: B
options.text: Raw TF counts cannot be stored in an inverted index

options.label: C
options.text: Raw TF values become negative for very high-frequency terms

options.label: D
options.text: Raw TF ignores whether a term appears in the query at all

questions.explanationMd: Long documents contain more words, so a term may occur more often simply because the document is longer, not because it is more focused on the query topic.

questions.questionMd: In the BM25 formula, what happens to document length normalization when the parameter `b` is set to 0?

options.label: A
options.text: Document length has no effect on the score and all documents are treated as having the same length

options.label: B
options.text: Document length is fully normalized and short documents are heavily favoured

options.label: C
options.text: BM25 reduces to a pure Boolean retrieval model with no frequency weighting

options.label: D
options.text: The parameter `avgdl` becomes the only length signal used in the formula

questions.explanationMd: `b=0` disables the document length normalization factor in BM25.

questions.questionMd: Levenshtein edit distance counts the minimum number of operations needed to transform one string into another. Which set of operations does it use?

options.label: A
options.text: Insert a character, delete a character, substitute one character

options.label: B
options.text: Substitute one character for another, transpose two adjacent characters, delete a character

options.label: C
options.text: Split a string, merge two strings, substitute one character for another

options.label: D
options.text: Insert a character, delete a character, transpose two adjacent characters

questions.explanationMd: Classic Levenshtein distance uses insertion, deletion, and substitution.

questions.questionMd: A proximity query is written as `term₁ /k term₂`. Which condition must hold in a candidate document for it to be included in the result?

options.label: A
options.text: The positional difference between `term₁` and `term₂` must be at most `k`

options.label: B
options.text: `term₁` must appear exactly `k` positions before `term₂` in every occurrence

options.label: C
options.text: The total count of `term₁` and `term₂` occurrences in the document must equal `k`

options.label: D
options.text: The terms must appear in the same sentence and within `k` paragraphs of each other

questions.explanationMd: A `/k` proximity operator requires the two terms to occur within `k` positions of each other.

questions.questionMd: In TREC relevance judging, Cohen's κ values typically fall between 0.6 and 0.8. What does this imply about IR evaluation?

options.label: A
options.text: The κ range shows that automated relevance labeling is more reliable than human judgment

options.label: B
options.text: Agreement is nearly perfect, so evaluation results can be treated as ground truth without reservation

options.label: C
options.text: There is substantial but imperfect agreement among assessors

options.label: D
options.text: Annotators disagree so frequently that per-query results are unreliable and should be discarded

questions.explanationMd: A κ value around 0.6–0.8 indicates substantial but not perfect human agreement.

questions.questionMd: A postings list for the term `orbit` contains the doc_ids `[3, 11, 22, 45, 56]`. What is the correct gap-encoded representation of this list?

options.label: C
options.text: [3, 11, 22, 45, 56] stored unchanged because the first value is already a gap

questions.explanationMd: Gap encoding stores the first docID and then differences: `3, 11-3=8, 22-11=11, 45-22=23, 56-45=11`.

questions.questionMd: A search application needs to find news articles about `space exploration` published after January 1, 2024, ranked by relevance. How should the date constraint be placed in the OpenSearch Query DSL to achieve the best performance?

options.label: A
options.text: In the `should` clause of a bool query, giving a score boost to articles published after the cutoff date

options.label: B
options.text: In the `must` clause of a bool query, so that it contributes positively to the relevance score for recent articles

options.label: C
options.text: In the `filter` clause of a bool query, because filter context is cached and does not affect the relevance score

options.label: D
options.text: As a top-level range query outside any bool wrapper, since date fields cannot be nested inside compound queries

questions.explanationMd: The date constraint is a non-scoring condition, so it belongs in filter context for caching and efficiency.

questions.questionMd: Under the TREC standard four-point graded relevance scale, which grade label is assigned to a document that is a perfect, exact answer to the query?

options.label: A
options.text: 1 — Partially relevant

options.label: B
options.text: 3 — Perfectly relevant

options.label: C
options.text: 2 — Highly relevant

options.label: D
options.text: 4 — Authoritative source

questions.explanationMd: The lecture scale uses grade 3 for a perfectly relevant document.

questions.questionMd: Recall measures which aspect of retrieval performance?

options.label: A
options.text: The average precision at each recall level across multiple queries

options.label: B
options.text: The rank position of the first relevant document in the result list

options.label: C
options.text: The fraction of retrieved documents that are relevant

options.label: D
options.text: The fraction of all relevant documents that were successfully retrieved

questions.explanationMd: Recall is relevant retrieved divided by all relevant documents.

questions.questionMd: When building a k-gram index for general English text information retrieval, which value of `k` is described as the recommended tradeoff between index size and retrieval precision?
questions.explanationMd: The lecture notes describe 3-grams as a common tradeoff between index size and candidate precision.

questions.questionMd: Which stemmer described in the lectures is characterized as the most aggressive, producing the smallest vocabulary but the highest over-stemming error rate?

options.label: A
options.text: Snowball

options.label: B
options.text: WordNet lemmatizer

options.label: C
options.text: Lancaster

options.label: D
options.text: Porter

questions.explanationMd: Lancaster stemming is known as more aggressive than Porter or Snowball.

questions.questionMd: In the SMART notation table, the augmented TF variant (symbol `a`) is defined as which of the following?

options.label: A
options.text: `1 + log(tf / max_tf(d))`

options.label: C
options.text: `tf / (tf + max_tf(d))`

options.label: D
options.text: `0.5 * log(tf) + 0.5 * max_tf(d)`

questions.explanationMd: The augmented TF formula scales raw TF by the maximum term frequency in the document and maps it into `[0.5, 1]`.

questions.questionMd: A standard IR test collection consists of exactly three required components. Which of the following correctly identifies all three?

options.label: A
options.text: A training set, a validation set, and a held-out test set

options.label: B
options.text: An inverted index, a stemmer, and a stop-word list

options.label: C
options.text: A fixed corpus, standardized topics, and human relevance judgments (qrels)

options.label: D
options.text: A ranked retrieval model, a query parser, and a relevance feedback module

questions.explanationMd: A classic IR test collection contains documents, topics/queries, and relevance judgments.

questions.questionMd: How does TF-IDF enable keyword extraction from a single document within a larger corpus?

options.label: A
options.text: Terms whose raw TF exceeds the collection average document frequency are selected as keywords regardless of their IDF value

options.label: B
options.text: Terms with the lowest TF-IDF weight are the best keywords because they are unique to the document and appear nowhere else

options.label: C
options.text: Terms with the highest TF-IDF weight in a document are strong candidate keywords for that document

options.label: D
options.text: Terms are selected as keywords when their IDF value equals zero, indicating they are universally recognized concepts

questions.explanationMd: High TF-IDF terms are frequent in the document but relatively distinctive in the collection, making them good keyword candidates.

questions.questionMd: A medical literature search system is designed to ensure clinicians find every relevant study on a drug interaction. Which evaluation metric is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: MRR, because clinicians only need to find the single most authoritative study for each query

options.label: B
options.text: NDCG@10, because graded relevance most accurately reflects a clinician's document preferences

options.label: C
options.text: P@5, because clinicians typically only read the first five results returned

options.label: D
options.text: MAP, because it rewards retrieving all relevant documents and penalises any that are missed

questions.explanationMd: When the goal is to retrieve all relevant studies, MAP is more suitable than single-result or top-k-only metrics because it considers relevant documents across the ranked list.

questions.questionMd: In IR significance testing, bootstrap resampling estimates confidence intervals by which procedure?

options.label: A
options.text: Randomly splitting the document corpus into halves and comparing system scores on each half

options.label: B
options.text: Repeatedly sampling queries with replacement from the evaluation set and recomputing the metric each time

options.label: C
options.text: Shuffling relevance judgments across queries to simulate a null distribution

options.label: D
options.text: Running the retrieval system multiple times with different random seeds and averaging the results

questions.explanationMd: Bootstrap resampling draws query samples with replacement and recomputes the metric to estimate uncertainty.

questions.questionMd: In Boolean retrieval, an OR query between two terms produces results by applying which set operation to their postings lists?

options.label: A
options.text: Set difference — documents containing the first term but not the second

options.label: B
options.text: Set complement — all documents not containing either term

options.label: C
options.text: Set intersection — documents containing both terms simultaneously

options.label: D
options.text: Set union — documents containing either term or both

questions.explanationMd: Boolean OR corresponds to the union of postings lists.

questions.questionMd: For which type of query is Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) the most appropriate evaluation metric?

options.label: A
options.text: E-discovery tasks where both high precision and high recall are legally required

options.label: B
options.text: Ad-hoc multi-document queries evaluated over a large corpus with hundreds of relevant documents

options.label: C
options.text: Navigational or single-answer queries where users care only about finding the first correct result

options.label: D
options.text: Medical literature searches requiring comprehensive coverage of all relevant studies

questions.explanationMd: MRR focuses on the rank of the first relevant result, so it is best for navigational or single-answer tasks.

questions.questionMd: A system has a high Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR). What does this indicate about its retrieval behavior?

options.label: A
options.text: The system retrieves all relevant documents within the top 10 results

options.label: B
options.text: The system maintains good Precision across a wide range of Recall levels simultaneously

options.label: C
options.text: The system's ranked list is longer than competitors, covering more of the corpus

options.label: D
options.text: The system has a very high Precision@1 but low Recall across all cutoffs

questions.explanationMd: High AUC-PR indicates strong precision is maintained as recall increases across many thresholds.

questions.questionMd: A corpus contains 1000 documents, and the term **quasar** appears in exactly 50 of them. Applying the formula `IDF(t) = log(N / df(t))`, what is the IDF of **quasar**?
questions.explanationMd: `N / df(t) = 1000 / 50 = 20`, so the IDF is `log(20)`, approximately `3.0` with natural logarithm.

questions.questionMd: The sentence **The cat sat on the mat** contains how many tokens and how many types respectively?

options.label: A
options.text: 6 tokens and 6 types

options.label: B
options.text: 5 tokens and 5 types

options.label: C
options.text: 5 tokens and 6 types

options.label: D
options.text: 6 tokens and 5 types

questions.explanationMd: There are 6 word occurrences: The, cat, sat, on, the, mat. Treating **The/the** as the same normalized word gives 5 distinct types.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is an accurate characterisation of relevance in information retrieval?

options.label: A
options.text: Relevance is graded, subjective, and context-dependent

options.label: B
options.text: Relevance is a fixed property of a document independent of who is asking

options.label: C
options.text: Two users with identical queries will always agree on which documents are relevant

options.label: D
options.text: Relevance is binary and can be determined algorithmically without human input

questions.explanationMd: In IR, relevance depends on the user's information need, context, and judgment; it may also be graded rather than simply binary.

questions.questionMd: The Ideal DCG (`IDCG@k`) is defined as the `DCG@k` of which ranking?

options.label: A
options.text: The ranking produced by the best-performing system in the evaluation pool

options.label: B
options.text: The theoretically perfect ranking, where all documents are sorted by descending relevance grade

options.label: C
options.text: The ranking that places all irrelevant documents first to establish a worst-case baseline

options.label: D
options.text: The ranking that maximizes Precision@k regardless of graded relevance

questions.explanationMd: IDCG is computed on the ideal ordering: documents are arranged by decreasing relevance grade to get the maximum possible DCG for that query.

questions.questionMd: A term has a document frequency (`DF`) of 500 and a term frequency (`TF`) of 12 in one particular document. What does the DF value of 500 indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: The term appears in 500 different documents in the corpus

options.label: B
options.text: The term appears in documents with an average length of 500 tokens

options.label: C
options.text: The term appears 500 times across all documents combined

options.label: D
options.text: The term's postings list contains 500 position entries

questions.explanationMd: Document frequency counts how many documents contain the term at least once, not how many total occurrences the term has.

questions.questionMd: According to SMART notation, which formula defines the logarithmic TF variant symbol `l` for a term with a non-zero count?

options.label: A
options.text: tf / (1 + log(tf))

options.label: B
options.text: log(tf) - 1

options.label: C
options.text: 1 + log(tf)

questions.explanationMd: In SMART notation, logarithmic term frequency weighting is commonly `1 + log(tf)` for non-zero term counts.

questions.questionMd: Why does the phrase query **"machine learning"** return fewer results than the Boolean query `machine AND learning`?

options.label: A
options.text: The phrase query additionally requires the two terms to appear consecutively in the correct order

options.label: B
options.text: The phrase query applies a Jaccard similarity threshold that the Boolean AND does not use

options.label: C
options.text: The phrase query restricts matching to document titles, whereas the Boolean AND searches the full text

options.label: D
options.text: The phrase query automatically removes stop words, reducing the candidate set before merging

questions.explanationMd: A phrase query is stricter than Boolean AND because it requires adjacency and order, not just the presence of both terms anywhere in the document.

questions.questionMd: A user searches **automobile fuel efficiency** but the most relevant document uses only the phrases **car gas mileage** and **vehicle consumption**. What problem does this scenario illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: The precision-recall tradeoff — retrieving more documents lowers average result quality

options.label: B
options.text: The stopword problem — common function words are masking the discriminating content terms

options.label: C
options.text: The vocabulary mismatch problem — lexical overlap is zero despite near-identical meaning

options.label: D
options.text: The corpus freshness problem — the index has not been updated to include recent terminology

questions.explanationMd: The query and document use different words for the same concept, so lexical matching may fail even though the meaning is similar.

questions.questionMd: How does a biword index handle a three-word phrase query such as **"machine learning model"**?

options.label: A
options.text: It decomposes the phrase into overlapping biwords and executes an AND query over machine_learning and learning_model

options.label: B
options.text: It falls back to a standard Boolean AND query over the three individual terms

options.label: C
options.text: It stores the entire three-word phrase as a single compound dictionary entry

options.label: D
options.text: It uses the positional index for any phrase longer than two words

questions.explanationMd: A biword index represents adjacent term pairs. A three-word phrase is converted into overlapping biwords, then both biword postings are intersected.

questions.questionMd: Given the ranked list `R, I, I, R, R` where R = relevant and I = irrelevant, what is the Average Precision (AP)?
questions.explanationMd: Relevant documents occur at ranks 1, 4, and 5. AP = (1/3)(1/1 + 2/4 + 3/5) = 0.700.

questions.questionMd: Which query structure correctly follows the best practice for using the NOT operator?

options.label: A
options.text: Replace every NOT operand with an equivalent OR over all other terms

options.label: B
options.text: Perform an AND merge first to reduce the candidate set, then apply NOT to the result

options.label: C
options.text: Lead the query with NOT to eliminate irrelevant documents before any AND merge

options.label: D
options.text: Apply NOT to the largest postings list to maximize the pruning effect

questions.explanationMd: NOT is best applied after positive terms have restricted the candidate set; leading with NOT can require scanning a very large complement.

questions.questionMd: Which formula correctly defines the F1 score in terms of Precision (P) and Recall (R)?

options.label: B
options.text: PR / (P + R)

options.label: D
options.text: 2PR / (P + R)

questions.explanationMd: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: `2PR / (P + R)`.

questions.questionMd: A corpus contains 1000 documents, and the term "quasar" appears in exactly 50 of them. Applying the formula `IDF(t) = log(N / df(t))`, what is the IDF of "quasar"?
questions.explanationMd: N/df = 1000/50 = 20, so the IDF is `log(20)`, approximately 3.0 using natural log.

questions.questionMd: In the text preprocessing pipeline, what is the correct order of stages?

options.label: A
options.text: Remove Stopwords → Tokenize → Normalize → Stem/Lemmatize → Index Terms

options.label: B
options.text: Tokenize → Normalize → Remove Stopwords → Stem/Lemmatize → Index Terms

options.label: C
options.text: Tokenize → Stem/Lemmatize → Normalize → Remove Stopwords → Index Terms

options.label: D
options.text: Normalize → Tokenize → Stem/Lemmatize → Remove Stopwords → Index Terms

questions.explanationMd: A typical pipeline first tokenizes text, normalizes tokens, removes stopwords, stems or lemmatizes terms, and then indexes them.

questions.questionMd: The two-pointer AND merge achieves O(m + n) time complexity only because of one crucial property of postings lists. What is that property?

options.label: A
options.text: Postings lists contain positional information for each document

options.label: B
options.text: Postings lists are stored in order of decreasing term frequency

options.label: C
options.text: Postings lists are stored in sorted order of document ID

options.label: D
options.text: Postings lists use variable-byte encoded gaps between document IDs

questions.explanationMd: Linear two-pointer intersection depends on both postings lists being sorted by document ID.

questions.questionMd: A term receives a high TF-IDF weight in a document when which condition holds?

options.label: A
options.text: The term appears rarely in that document but frequently across the overall collection

options.label: B
options.text: The term has a low IDF value and a high document frequency

options.label: C
options.text: The term appears in every document in the collection

options.label: D
options.text: The term appears frequently in that document but rarely across the overall collection

questions.explanationMd: High TF-IDF requires both high term frequency in the document and high IDF, meaning the term is rare across the collection.

questions.questionMd: In gap (delta) encoding of a postings list, how is the very first entry in the list stored?

options.label: A
options.text: As the absolute document ID, not as a gap

options.label: B
options.text: As a special sentinel value indicating the beginning of the list

options.label: C
options.text: As a gap of zero to signal the start of the list

options.label: D
options.text: As the difference between the first and second document IDs

questions.explanationMd: Since there is no previous document ID before the first posting, the first entry is stored directly as the absolute document ID.

questions.questionMd: A user searches "automobile fuel efficiency" but the most relevant document uses only the phrases "car gas mileage" and "vehicle consumption". What problem does this scenario illustrate?

options.label: A
options.text: The precision-recall tradeoff — retrieving more documents lowers average result quality

options.label: B
options.text: The vocabulary mismatch problem — lexical overlap is zero despite near-identical meaning

options.label: C
options.text: The corpus freshness problem — the index has not been updated to include recent terminology

options.label: D
options.text: The stopword problem — common function words are masking the discriminating content terms

questions.explanationMd: The query and document use different words for the same concept, so exact lexical matching can fail despite semantic similarity.

questions.questionMd: A student runs a Porter stemmer and observes that both "universe" and "university" produce the stem "univers". This is an example of which failure mode?

options.label: A
options.text: Over-stemming, which reduces retrieval precision

options.label: B
options.text: Accent folding, which merges morphologically unrelated forms

questions.explanationMd: Over-stemming merges terms that should remain distinct, which can increase false matches and reduce precision.

questions.questionMd: Zipf's Law states that the frequency of the r-th most common word is proportional to 1/r. If the most frequent term in a corpus appears 10,000 times, approximately how often does the 100th most frequent term appear?

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately 10 times

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 1,000 times

options.label: C
options.text: Approximately 100 times

options.label: D
options.text: Approximately 5,000 times

questions.explanationMd: Using frequency ≈ 10000 / r, the 100th term appears about 10000 / 100 = 100 times.

questions.questionMd: System A has MAP = 0.42 and System B has MAP = 0.43. A Wilcoxon signed-rank test yields p = 0.21. What is the correct conclusion?

options.label: A
options.text: System A is preferred because p > 0.05 confirms its stability across queries

options.label: B
options.text: The difference is not statistically significant

options.label: C
options.text: The test is invalid because the MAP difference is smaller than the p-value

options.label: D
options.text: System B is statistically and practically superior because it has a higher MAP score

questions.explanationMd: With p = 0.21, the difference does not meet a typical 0.05 significance threshold, so the observed MAP difference is not statistically significant.

questions.questionMd: A ranked list has graded relevance scores `[3, 1, 0, 2, 1]` at ranks 1 through 5. What is the approximate DCG@5?

options.label: A
options.text: 7.00, computed by summing the raw relevance grades 3+1+0+2+1

options.label: B
options.text: 2.50, computed as the arithmetic mean of the five relevance grades

options.label: C
options.text: 3.00, because only the first rank contributes and its grade is 3

questions.explanationMd: DCG discounts relevance by log2(rank+1): 3/1 + 1/log2(3) + 0/log2(4) + 2/log2(5) + 1/log2(6) ≈ 4.879.
